title: India Face Japan in Historic First-Ever T20I at Sano
excerpt: World No. 1 India warm up for the Asian Games against 41st-ranked Japan in a first-ever men's T20I at Sano, branded the Suzuki Cup — after rain washed out India's practice session and with no reserve day available.
body:
• India play Japan in a first-ever senior men's T20I — the Suzuki Cup — on Tuesday 22 September at Sano International Cricket Ground, starting 9:30 AM IST (1:00 PM JST).
  • World No. 1 India, led by Shreyas Iyer, warm up for the Asian Games 2026 men's T20 competition under head coach VVS Laxman, while 41st-ranked Japan view the match as the biggest moment in their cricket history.
  • Japan head coach Dhugal Bedingfield praised India's willingness to play: "Not every team would," and said India's tour "lift[s] everyone else up to make cricket a global sport."
  • India's training session was rained off on a wet outfield at Sano with a typhoon south of Japan a live threat; there is no reserve day because the Asian Games begin two days later. JioStar holds TV rights in India, FanCode has digital streaming.

India take on Japan in a first-ever senior men's T20I at the Sano International Cricket Ground in Tochigi Prefecture on Tuesday 22 September — a fixture both boards are branding the Suzuki Cup, and a rare warm-up contest the world champions accepted in the middle of a congested schedule.

Play begins at 9:30 AM IST (1:00 PM local time). For India, world No. 1 in T20Is and the reigning T20 World Cup champions after defending their title earlier this year, it is the final tune-up before the Asian Games 2026 men's T20 cricket competition opens in Aichi-Nagoya two days later. For Japan, ranked 41st, it is the most significant fixture the country has ever hosted — and its players, most of whom hold full-time jobs or are students, are treating it that way.

Sport 75 and 75 years of India-Japan ties

The fixture is part of the "Sport 75" initiative marking 75 years of India-Japan diplomatic relations, which are formally celebrated in 2027. According to Japan coach Dhugal Bedingfield, the match came together in barely a month — "Absolutely 100 percent" a surprise, he said — and he believes the conversation went all the way up to prime-ministerial level in both countries.

Cricket's foothold in Japan remains small, competing for young athletes against baseball and soccer. The Japan Cricket Association has positioned this match as a shop window: show the sport at its best, in front of the best, and on home turf. Tickets sold out within hours, and the venue has been upgraded with a relaid turf square, temporary seating, ticket gates and heightened security.

Bedingfield: "Not every team would"

"Credit to the Indian team for agreeing to play. Not every team would. I get a sense from India that they're not lowering themselves by playing Japan, but trying to lift everyone else up to make cricket a global sport."

— Dhugal Bedingfield, Japan head coach

Bedingfield told the Indian Express the mood inside his camp — in training since Thursday — was excitement, not awe. On the gulf between the sides, he was realistic about modern T20 cricket: "The way T20s play these days by the best teams, not just India, is you can get blown out of the water by just the firepower of some of these players."

His focus, he said, is resilience — how Japan bounce back inside a game and how they stop the occasion overwhelming them. Japan's players are part-timers: most work full- or part-time jobs or study, receiving at best an allowance on tour and a couple of meals. Cricket in Japan survives on that volunteer economy, and Tuesday is the payoff for it.

Rain disruption and no reserve day

India's preparations were hit before a ball was bowled. A wet, soft outfield at Sano forced the cancellation of India's practice session, and JCA chief operating officer Alan Curr warned about the ground conditions as the BCCI posted "Touchdown Tokyo" on the team's arrival on 21 September. A typhoon south of Japan remains an active risk through the match window.

There is no reserve day. With the Asian Games T20 competition starting on 24 September — Japan open against Afghanistan in the group stage while Shreyas Iyer's India enter directly at the quarter-final stage — the calendar leaves no room. If rain wins, the historic occasion simply passes without one.

How to watch

JioStar holds the television broadcast rights in India, with FanCode carrying digital streaming. ITW Universe holds the exclusive global production, broadcast distribution and commercial marketing rights for the match. "India playing Japan on Japanese soil for the very first time is a monumental moment for global cricket," said JCA chief executive Naoki Alex Miyaji. Umpires are New Zealand's Chris Brown and Japan's Chris Thurgate.

Squads and the road to the Asian Games

India are led by captain Shreyas Iyer, with Tilak Varma as vice-captain, and coached by VVS Laxman for the Asian Games assignment — regular head coach Gautam Gambhir stayed back to oversee the ODI series against West Indies starting 27 September. The squad includes Jasprit Bumrah, Arshdeep Singh, Sanju Samson, Ishan Kishan, Abhishek Sharma, Axar Patel, Shivam Dube, Washington Sundar, Ravi Bishnoi, Yash Thakur and teenage opener Vaibhav Sooryavanshi. Varun Chakravarthy was ruled out on 16 September with a side strain and replaced by Vipraj Nigam.

Japan are captained by Kendel Kadowaki-Fleming. Win or lose on Tuesday, they carry the experience straight into Aichi-Nagoya — the first dividend of a fixture that, two months of organising notwithstanding, nobody in Japanese cricket expected to happen at all.
image_caption: Indian players celebrate during a T20 International. The reigning T20 World Cup champions face Japan in a first-ever men's T20I at the Sano International Cricket Ground on Tuesday 22 September, branded the Suzuki Cup.
nri_angle: For the Indian diaspora in Japan — one of Asia's fastest-growing Indian communities — Tuesday's match is a rare homecoming of Indian cricket on Japanese soil, while fans in India get a morning fixture that doubles as a cultural bridge between two partner nations.
author: Diaspora Desk
